performers: London Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Three rising notes in the strings grow into the finale’s great D major tune. Pierre Monteux and the London Symphony Orchestra play the complete symphony, including the long crescendo that carries the scherzo straight into the finale.

sections.label: A · I. Strings rise three notes
sections.mNote: Short string phrases answered by woodwinds and horns

sections.label: B · Woodwinds after a pause
sections.mNote: A longer woodwind phrase interrupts the opening dance

sections.label: Dev · Plucked strings
sections.mNote: Pizzicato introduces the development’s short, unsettled phrases

sections.label: Dev · Quiet winds gather speed
sections.mNote: Woodwind phrases draw the opening ideas into a crescendo

sections.label: A′ · Two themes together
sections.mNote: The opening themes return together in counterpoint

sections.label: Coda · The opening dance returns
sections.mNote: The first movement ends with its quiet string phrases

sections.mNote: Cellos and basses pluck a path for the bassoon melody

sections.label: C′ · The bassoon tune grows fiercer
sections.mNote: The opening tune expands towards the brass climax

sections.label: D · A long melody for strings
sections.mNote: Divided strings sing the contrasting theme

sections.label: C″ · The dark march returns
sections.mNote: The bassoon theme returns as a heavy processional

sections.label: D′ · The string melody climbs
sections.mNote: The quiet string theme returns and grows through interruptions

sections.label: E · Broken phrases after the climax

sections.label: Coda · Another climb, two plucked notes
sections.mNote: The slow movement gathers again and ends with pizzicato

sections.mNote: Fast string figures underneath longer wind phrases

sections.label: I · The darker march

cues.title: Three notes in the strings
cues.text: The strings begin with three rising notes in D major. Woodwinds and horns answer in short phrases, with room between them. These modest beginnings contain the outline of the great tune that will fill the finale.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, account of Symphony No. 2, first-movement discussion and score extract 7; the finale discussion identifies the returning three-note figure. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Don Juan at Rapallo
cues.text: In February 1901, Sibelius is in Rapallo, Italy, sketching a theme for the slow movement. Beside it he writes a scene for Don Juan: a stranger enters his castle and refuses to answer. When the stranger sings, Don Juan recognises Death.
cues.evidence: The Rapallo sketches and their Don Juan association are described by the Sibelius Society of Finland: https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . The sketch’s prose is reproduced at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius).

cues.title: Two themes share the room
cues.text: The opening dance and the longer woodwind theme return together. Sibelius fits them against one another in counterpoint: one phrase can keep moving while the other sings across it. The scattered beginnings have found company.
cues.evidence: Paul Serotsky’s score-based programme note describes the first movement’s recapitulation with both main subjects together in counterpoint. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Plucked steps, a bassoon song
cues.text: The slow movement opens in D minor. Cellos and basses pluck a long line before the bassoons begin their sombre song. Each low note sounds like another step towards the door.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 8: pizzicato cellos and double basses, then bassoon theme. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . D minor: IMSLP work catalogue, https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.2,_Op.43_(Sibelius,_Jean).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings after the brass
cues.text: After the brass climax and a pause, divided strings unfold a long, quiet melody. Sibelius labels its early sketch “Christus”. Its calm is repeatedly interrupted as the movement continues.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 9, identifies the Christus sketch; divided-string scoring and the preceding brass climax are described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Helsinki, then Stockholm
cues.text: Sibelius conducts the première in Helsinki on 8 March 1902. He revises the symphony afterwards; his brother-in-law Armas Järnefelt conducts the new version in Stockholm on 10 November 1903.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland gives both premières, conductors and versions. Armas Järnefelt is Aino Sibelius’s brother. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

cues.title: Strings at full tilt
cues.text: The scherzo sends the strings racing through rapid repeated figures. Slower wind phrases ride above them; the flute can sound remarkably unhurried while the bows are working furiously below.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, scherzo discussion and score extract 10: fast string figures under the flute theme. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nine notes from the oboe
cues.text: The trio slows the dance into G♭ major. An oboe repeats the same note nine times, supported by clarinets and horns, before its melody opens out. So little changes, and suddenly everything feels tender.
cues.evidence: Nine repeated notes: Sibelius Society of Finland, score extract 11, https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . G♭ major and clarinet-and-horn accompaniment: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius).
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trumpets answer in D
cues.text: The scherzo’s long crescendo carries straight into the finale. Strings sing the three-note rise in D major, broad and unashamed; trumpets answer where woodwinds answered in the first movement. The little opening dance has grown to fill the orchestra.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, bridge and finale discussion, score extract 12: rising figure, D major strings and trumpet answer. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm . The continuous join is also documented in the recording’s movement list: https://archive.org/details/sibelius-2-compl-monteux-lso .
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One more step upward
cues.text: The closing D major music draws out the rising figure once more. Late in this coda, its familiar three notes finally reach a fourth. Sibelius has saved that extra step for the last great stretch of the symphony.
cues.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, final-movement discussion, credits Erkki Salmenhaara with identifying the late extension of the three-note figure. The cue covers the coda as a whole. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A pause leaves room for woodwinds
transitions.from: A · I. Strings rise three notes
transitions.how: The opening dance stops for a pause. Woodwinds take up a longer, more insistent phrase, changing the scale of the melody after the strings’ short, separated answers.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion: pause, then the woodwind second-subject group. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: Plucked strings begin the next argument
transitions.how: Pizzicato strings begin the development. A rocking phrase and short woodwind figures grow around them, while the opening string rhythm keeps returning beneath the new phrases.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion: pizzicato at the development, rocking phrase, woodwind theme and continuing opening accompaniment. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: The two themes return together
transitions.how: The crescendo relaxes, and the opening dance returns alongside the longer woodwind phrase. Their different rhythms fit together in counterpoint; Sibelius lets both themes speak at once.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, first-movement discussion of the recapitulation. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: D major closes; plucked D minor begins
transitions.to: C · II. Plucked basses and bassoons
transitions.how: The first movement closes quietly in D major. After the break, cellos and basses begin the slow movement in D minor, plucking a long line before the bassoons join. The marking is Tempo andante, ma rubato: a walking pace, freely shaped.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, first- and second-movement discussions; movement keys and heading in the IMSLP work catalogue. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm ; https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.2,_Op.43_(Sibelius,_Jean)

transitions.title: Divided strings answer the brass
transitions.from: C′ · The bassoon tune grows fiercer
transitions.to: D · A long melody for strings
transitions.how: The brass climax stops, leaving a pause. Divided strings begin the contrasting melody quietly, with long phrases in place of the preceding broken calls. Sibelius’s sketch for this theme bears the heading “Christus”.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, second-movement discussion and score extract 9; scoring and pause described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: The bass breaks the long melody
transitions.to: E · Broken phrases after the climax
transitions.how: The long string melody reaches its climax, then the contrary phrase in the bass interrupts its progress. The music breaks into quiet fragments, recalling pieces of the earlier tune.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, second-movement discussion: the second theme’s climax is interrupted by its bass variant before the fragmentary coda. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: Two plucked notes, then racing bows
transitions.from: Coda · Another climb, two plucked notes
transitions.how: Two pizzicato strokes end the slow movement. After the break, Vivacissimo sends the strings into fast repeated figures, with longer woodwind phrases above them. The bows have scarcely time to rest.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, slow-movement ending and scherzo discussion, score extract 10. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: The oboe holds the dance still
transitions.how: The fast string figures stop. The trio settles into G♭ major, and an oboe repeats one note nine times over clarinets and horns. The melody opens gradually out of that repeated note.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, score extract 11; G♭ major and accompaniment described at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._2_(Sibelius). https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: The horns add a rising figure
transitions.to: F′ · Fast strings and rising horns
transitions.how: The scherzo resumes its fast string figures. Sibelius changes the slower phrases above them and adds a rising horn figure. The same scurrying accompaniment now carries a new call across it.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, scherzo discussion: altered slower phrases and new rising horn figure in the return. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: The slow oboe tune comes back
transitions.from: F′ · Fast strings and rising horns
transitions.how: The strings’ rapid figures subside and the slow trio comes back. The oboe melody returns to the foreground. This time the trio continues into the rising bridge to the finale.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, scherzo and finale discussion: second trio and continuous transition. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

transitions.title: G♭, A♭, B♭ begin the climb
transitions.how: The trio becomes a crescendo built around G♭–A♭–B♭. The three rising notes recall the shape heard at the beginning of the symphony. Repetition lengthens the climb until the finale’s D major tune can break through.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland identifies G♭–A♭–B♭ as the bridge motif and D major as the finale’s arrival. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm

transitions.title: D major without a break
transitions.to: H · IV. Strings answered by trumpets
transitions.how: The crescendo carries straight into D major. Strings sing the three-note rise as a broad melody; trumpets answer. The finale’s Allegro moderato opens out from the bridge, with no silence between the movements.
transitions.evidence: Sibelius Society of Finland, finale discussion and score extract 12; the recording’s movement list also specifies the continuous join. https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_sinf_02.htm ; https://archive.org/details/sibelius-2-compl-monteux-lso

transitions.title: Woodwinds crowd around the returning tune
transitions.from: J · The oboe in a hush
transitions.to: H′ · The string tune gathers strength
transitions.how: The quiet passage begins a long crescendo towards the return of the broad string tune. Short woodwind figures gather around the melody, keeping their sharper rhythm against its long phrases.
transitions.evidence: Paul Serotsky, finale discussion: gradual build to the main theme’s reprise with active woodwind figures. https://www.musicweb-international.com/Programme_Notes/sibelius_sym2.htm

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both the Internet Archive description and the Decca booklet credit the London Symphony Orchestra under Monteux. The leader and principals on this session are not documented here; the booklet’s essay says that Hugh Maguire joined as leader after the orchestra’s 1957 arrival of young players, without tying that to this date.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: The 1903 final version, as published by Fazer & Westerlund (the version in general use); the performing edition of this recording has not been checked against a score
fields.note: The Sibelius Society gives the first version (premiere 8 March 1902) and the final version of 1903. The 1958 recording would normally use the published score; the Decca booklet lists Breitkopf & Härtel as publisher of the edition. No source states which version Monteux used, and no score alignment was made.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The Decca booklet gives Kingsway Hall, 18–20 June 1958, for the disc whose track list holds this symphony (PDF page 21, printed p. 40, beside the track list on PDF page 20, printed p. 39; the 24 and 25 June 1958 sessions marked with an asterisk are for Elgar’s Enigma Variations on the same disc). The Internet Archive description narrows the date to 20 June 1958 without a source. The identification rests on the layout of the booklet’s credits, which the author read as attaching to the disc listing Sibelius and Elgar; the measured movement lengths of this file (10:17, 14:36, 6:14 and 12:49) match the booklet’s track times (10:16, 14:36, 6:15, 12:49).

fields.label: Label
fields.value: RCA (US catalogue LSC 2342; UK catalogue SB 207); Decca reissue SDD 234 (September 1970)
fields.note: The booklet’s “First released as” line names the catalogue numbers and months but not the label name for SB 207. The Internet Archive description says Decca–RCA. The author treats the first issue as RCA’s.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The first issue was in October 1959 (LSC 2342) and May 1960 (SB 207); both dates are before 1963.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The booklet names no matrix, take or side numbers.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The Internet Archive item was uploaded by a private account (subject tag “DWTKenInNY”); its description names no transfer engineer or source disc.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s public date is 11 June 2023; that is an upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: A single VBR MP3 of the whole symphony; the uploader’s movement times are given in the description
fields.note: The Internet Archive derivative is a 78.7 MB VBR MP3 lasting 2,637 seconds. Whether it was sourced from an LP, CD or tape is not stated. No further processing is disclosed.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Sibelius died in 1957, so the symphony (published 1903) is in copyright in countries with a life-plus-70 term, including the EU, until the end of 2027; IMSLP records it as public domain in the United States, Canada and life-plus-50 countries
fields.note: The IMSLP work page carries a notice that the work is not in the public domain in life-plus-70 countries. The end date of 2027 is computed from Sibelius’s death in 1957, which the site’s Sibelius biography gives as 20 September 1957. This dossier does not claim the composition is out of copyright in the EU. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording, not the composition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — EU public domain (territorial): first published before 1963 (RCA LSC 2342, October 1959; SB 207, May 1960).
fields.note: Territorial only: the recording’s first publication in 1959–60 predates 1963, so its EU 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. The United States status of a 1958–59 sound recording is not established here. The Internet Archive item carries no licence URL; its metadata and description contain no non-commercial restriction. The item belongs to a general “folksoundomy” collection and was uploaded by a third party, not by the rights holder.

dossier.credit: Jean Sibelius, Symphony No. 2 in D major, Op. 43. London Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux, conductor. Recorded at Kingsway Hall, London, 18–20 June 1958; first issued as RCA LSC 2342 (1959). Single-file Internet Archive upload, item sibelius-2-compl-monteux-lso. Territorial public-domain basis (first published before 1963).

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: He watched sixteen swans circle over Ainola, gave their flight to the horns, and spent four years getting the Fifth Symphony right.
facts: Wegelius in Helsinki, 1885–89; Becker in Berlin; Fuchs and Goldmark in Vienna
Ainola, Lars Sonck’s timber house near Lake Tuusula, from 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish at school and in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven symphonies, one violin concerto, tone poems, theatre music, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
In Vienna in 1891, Sibelius auditioned for the Philharmonic and failed. He wanted to be a violinist; the jury found him too nervous even for an orchestral post. He was twenty-five, studying composition with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark, spending money he did not have at parties and taking in as much music as the city could offer. After hearing Bruckner’s Third Symphony he thought its author the greatest living composer. Meanwhile, in his lodgings, he was studying the rhythms of the Finnish Kalevala.

He had been born in Hämeenlinna in 1865, when Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire. His father, a doctor, died three years later, leaving debts. At home the family spoke Swedish; at school Janne learnt Finnish. He played chamber music with his sister Linda and brother Christian, and in 1885 went to Helsinki, nominally to study law. Martin Wegelius’s Music Institute soon claimed his days. There he befriended Ferruccio Busoni and worked through quartets by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. His professional name came cheaply: he found a dead uncle’s visiting cards. “Jean is now my musical name,” he told Uncle Pehr on 31 March 1886. Studies with Albert Becker in Berlin followed Helsinki, then came Vienna.
